stem: Which OSI layer is the only one that appends both a header and a trailer to the data it receives from the layer above?
explanation: The data-link layer wraps the network-layer packet in a frame header and adds a trailer holding the frame check sequence. No other layer attaches a trailer, which makes the frame the only PDU with fields at both ends.

choices.text: Data link
Network
Transport
Session

stem: Which OSI layer defines the voltage levels, connector types, and pin assignments used on a cable?
explanation: The physical layer is the only layer concerned with the mechanical and electrical specification of the medium. Voltages, pinouts, and connector shapes are all physical-layer details; framing and addressing sit above it.

choices.text: Physical
Data link
Network
Transport

stem: An IPv6 packet carries a Next Header value of 58. Which protocol does the payload contain?
explanation: Value 58 identifies ICMPv6. ICMPv6 carries neighbour discovery, router advertisements, and echo messages, and it is the protocol most IPv6 control-plane functions depend on. TCP is 6 and UDP is 17.

choices.text: ICMPv6
TCP
UDP
OSPFv3

stem: How many bits long is the Flow Label field in the IPv6 base header?
explanation: The Flow Label is 20 bits, sitting between the 8-bit Traffic Class and the 16-bit Payload Length. Its combined field of Traffic Class plus Flow Label occupies 28 bits, leaving the version nibble to complete the first 32-bit word.

choices.text: 20 bits
8 bits
16 bits
32 bits

stem: Which statement describes the difference between SC and LC fiber connectors?
explanation: SC uses a square push-pull body with a 2.5 mm ferrule, while LC is roughly half the size, uses a 1.25 mm ferrule, and latches like an RJ-style clip. LC therefore allows roughly double the port density on a patch panel.

choices.text: LC is smaller and latches, SC is larger and pushes straight in
SC is smaller and latches, LC is larger and pushes straight in
Both use a 1.25 mm ferrule and differ only in colour
SC is used only for single-mode and LC only for multimode

stem: What does a cable category rating such as Cat 6 actually specify?
explanation: A category rating specifies the maximum frequency the cable must support and the associated insertion loss, crosstalk, and return-loss limits. It does not mandate a particular Ethernet speed; a standard such as 1000BASE-T is what maps a speed onto a category.

choices.text: The maximum frequency and performance limits the cable must meet
The maximum cable length that the standard permits
The exact Ethernet speed the cable will always run at
The shielding material used around each conductor pair

stem: How does an out-of-band management network reach a switch that has lost all data-plane connectivity?
explanation: Out-of-band management connects each device console or aux port to a terminal server, giving a path that does not depend on the production network. Because it uses a separate physical and logical path, it still works when the data plane, routing, or the device IP stack is broken.

choices.text: Through the console or aux port wired to a terminal server
Through an SSH session to the management SVI
Through the loopback address reachable over the routed core
Through an SNMP trap sent to the NMS server

stem: In a routed-access campus design, where does the Layer 2 domain end?
explanation: In routed access the access switch itself is the Layer 3 gateway, so the Layer 2 boundary is the access switch uplink. Every uplink to the distribution or core layer is a routed point-to-point link, which removes spanning tree from the campus and shrinks each failure domain to a single closet.

choices.text: At the access switch uplink, which is a routed point-to-point link
At the distribution switch trunk toward the core
At the core switch where VLANs are terminated
At the WAN edge router interface

stem: A single link between one leaf and one spine fails in a spine-leaf fabric running ECMP. What is the result?
explanation: Equal-cost multipathing simply removes the failed path from the hash and spreads flows across the remaining spines. There is no blocked port and no spanning-tree reconvergence, so traffic keeps flowing with only the fabric bisection bandwidth reduced.

choices.text: Traffic is rehashed over the remaining equal-cost paths with no STP event
Spanning tree blocks the leaf uplink and reconverges over 30 seconds
The leaf loses all connectivity until the link is restored
The fabric elects a new root bridge for that leaf

stem: Why is VXLAN typically used on top of a spine-leaf fabric?
explanation: VXLAN builds a Layer 2 overlay across a Layer 3 underlay, so segments can span racks and workloads can move without re-addressing. The underlay stays a simple routed fabric where every spine-to-leaf link is forwarding, and the overlay carries the large tenant address space.

choices.text: It provides a Layer 2 overlay over the Layer 3 underlay for large segments
It replaces the need for a routing protocol in the underlay
It removes the need for MAC address learning on the leaf switches
It compresses tenant traffic so fewer uplinks are needed

stem: A container is deleted and recreated from the same image. Which mechanism keeps its data across that cycle?
explanation: A persistent volume is storage provisioned outside the container filesystem and mounted into it. Because the volume lifecycle is independent of the container, recreating the container reattaches the same data, whereas the writable layer of the old container is discarded.

choices.text: A persistent volume mounted into the container
The writable layer inside the old container
The container image itself
The container runtime cache

stem: A hypervisor is configured to run virtual machines whose combined RAM allocation exceeds the physical memory installed. What makes this possible?
explanation: Memory overcommit relies on the hypervisor reclaiming pages that guests have not touched, using ballooning, transparent page sharing, and swapping to a datastore. It works because guests rarely use every allocated byte at the same moment; if they do, performance collapses or the host runs out of memory.

choices.text: The hypervisor reclaims idle guest pages through ballooning and swapping
Each guest is given a private copy of physical RAM on demand
The CPU throttles guests so their memory needs shrink
The guest operating systems share a single kernel address space

stem: In a service provider WAN, which device is the customer edge?
explanation: The customer edge is the equipment on the customer premises that hands off to the provider, typically a router or firewall owned or managed by the customer. The provider edge is the provider-owned device on the other end of that handoff link.

choices.text: The customer-owned device that hands off to the provider network
The provider device that terminates the customer access circuit
The provider backbone router inside the core
The internet exchange switch shared by many providers

stem: Which MEF service type gives a customer any-to-any connectivity among three or more sites?
explanation: E-LAN is a multipoint-to-multipoint service, so every site can reach every other site through a single logical LAN. E-Line is point-to-point, and E-Tree is rooted multipoint where leaves may only talk to the root.

choices.text: E-LAN, a multipoint-to-multipoint service
E-Line, a point-to-point service
E-Tree, a rooted multipoint service
A dedicated leased line per site pair

stem: An email gateway flags an attachment as suspicious but cannot identify it from signatures. Which control determines whether it is malicious before delivery?
explanation: A sandbox executes the file in an isolated instrumented environment and observes what it attempts to do, such as writing to autorun keys or contacting a command-and-control host. Behavioural detonation catches unknown malware that signature matching cannot classify.

choices.text: Detonating the file in an isolated sandbox and watching its behaviour
Matching the file hash against the antivirus signature database
Blocking the attachment based on its file extension
Quarantining every attachment that contains macros

stem: Why must an inline intrusion prevention system decrypt TLS sessions to inspect them?
explanation: TLS hides the application payload from anything between the endpoints, so an inline sensor sees only ciphertext and record headers. Decryption, typically through a trusted certificate on the sensor, restores the plaintext the signature engine needs; without it the device can only profile metadata.

choices.text: The payload is ciphertext, so signatures cannot match without decryption
The sensor needs the session keys to forward packets upstream
Decryption is required to preserve the packet ordering
TLS resets the connection when a passive device observes it

stem: What distinguishes a public subnet from a private subnet in a cloud VPC?
explanation: A public subnet has a route table entry pointing default traffic at an internet gateway, so resources with public addresses are reachable from the internet. A private subnet has no such route and relies on a NAT device for outbound-only access.

choices.text: Its route table points to an internet gateway
It uses a different private address range
It has a larger CIDR block than a private subnet
Its security groups allow inbound traffic by default

stem: Which cloud addressing feature provides a static public IPv4 address that can be detached from one instance and attached to another?
explanation: An elastic IP is allocated to the account rather than to an instance, so it can be remapped during failover while clients keep using the same destination address. A normal public address is tied to the instance and released when the instance stops.

choices.text: An elastic IP address
A public IPv4 address assigned at launch
A private address in the VPC CIDR
A carrier-grade NAT address from the provider

stem: What is the default VTP operating mode on a Cisco switch?
explanation: A switch with no explicit VTP configuration runs in server mode. That is why a new switch with the null domain can join an existing domain and receive the VLAN database, which is also why a stray server can overwrite VLANs across the domain.

choices.text: Server
Client
Transparent
Off

stem: Two switches are connected by a trunk and both run VTP server mode, but their VTP domain names differ. What happens?
explanation: VTP updates are only accepted from neighbours in the same domain name, so with mismatched names the two databases stay independent. Each switch keeps its own VLAN list and neither synchronises, even though the trunk itself passes traffic normally.

choices.text: Each switch keeps its own VLAN database and no updates are exchanged
The switch with the higher revision number overwrites the other
The domain name is negotiated and both adopt the lower value
The trunk fails because VTP domain mismatch blocks 802.1Q

stem: Which two pieces of information does a DTP frame carry that let neighbours decide whether to form a trunk?
explanation: DTP advertises the sender VTP domain name and the desired trunk status, along with the neighbour identity and a timestamp. The domain field keeps unrelated switches from negotiating with each other, and the status field drives the auto and desirable state machine.

choices.text: The VTP domain name and the desired trunk status
The native VLAN and the allowed VLAN list
The spanning-tree priority and the bridge ID
The port speed and the duplex setting

stem: A port is left in DTP dynamic auto mode. How does it behave?
explanation: Dynamic auto waits passively: it will answer a trunk request from a desirable neighbour but never starts the negotiation itself. Two dynamic auto ports therefore settle as access ports, which is the usual cause of a trunk that will not come up.

choices.text: It responds to trunk requests but never initiates negotiation
It initiates negotiation every 30 seconds until a trunk forms
It always becomes a trunk regardless of the neighbour
It disables DTP and stays a permanent access port

stem: How does a multilayer switch derive the MAC address it uses for its switched virtual interfaces?
explanation: All SVIs share the switch chassis base MAC burned into the backplane; the SVI does not get a per-interface address. Because every SVI presents the same MAC, a host that moves between VLANs on the same switch still sees one consistent gateway MAC.

choices.text: It reuses the chassis base MAC for every SVI
It allocates a random MAC per VLAN at boot
It inherits the MAC of the first port in the VLAN
It queries a pool of MAC addresses from the supervisor

stem: A switch rejects the command `interface vlan 20` with an address that belongs to the same subnet as VLAN 10. Why?
explanation: The configuration is refused because two SVIs cannot hold addresses in the same subnet; each VLAN interface must own a distinct connected network. Overlapping subnets would make the CEF table ambiguous about which interface reaches a destination.

choices.text: Two VLAN interfaces cannot have addresses in the same subnet
VLAN 20 must be created before an SVI can be configured
The address is in the reserved 10.0.0.0/8 range
The switch only supports one SVI at a time

stem: A host on VLAN 30 must send a packet to a destination in VLAN 40 on the same multilayer switch. What MAC address does the host place in the frame?
explanation: The host compares the destination with its own subnet mask, sees a different network, and ARPs for its default gateway. The reply carries the SVI MAC, so the frame is addressed to the switch, which rewrites the Layer 2 header before forwarding into VLAN 40.

choices.text: The MAC of its default gateway SVI
The MAC of the destination host in VLAN 40
The broadcast address FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF
The chassis base MAC of the destination switch

stem: A switch without PoE support must power an 802.3af access point. What device solves this?
explanation: A midspan injector sits on the cable between the switch and the powered device and adds power to the spare pairs or through the data pairs. The switch keeps sending ordinary Ethernet while the injector supplies the 48 V, so no switch replacement is needed.

choices.text: A midspan power injector placed between the switch and the device
A crossover cable wired to pass power
A PoE splitter at the switch end of the cable
An inline UPS on the switch uplink

stem: Why do standards limit the power delivered per port when many PoE cables are bundled together?
explanation: Bundled cables trap heat, and the resulting temperature rise increases conductor resistance beyond what a single free-air cable would see. The bundle derating rules reduce the permitted current per pair so the insulation temperature rating is not exceeded.

choices.text: Trapped heat in the bundle raises conductor temperature and requires derating
The switch power supply cannot deliver power to adjacent ports
Bundled cables couple data signals and cause CRC errors
PoE detection fails when cables touch each other

stem: Two virtual machines on different ESXi hosts are configured with the same port group name and VLAN. How does their traffic reach each other?
explanation: The virtual switch is local to each host, so the frame leaves through the host physical NIC and crosses the physical network. It arrives on the other host and is delivered by that host virtual switch to the destination VM; the shared port group name only keeps the VLAN and policy consistent.

choices.text: It leaves the host NIC and crosses the physical network to the other host
It stays inside the local virtual switch of the first host
It is forwarded by the hypervisor kernel over a shared memory channel
It is dropped because port groups are host-local

stem: Why is the MTU on the physical NIC and the virtual switch raised when VXLAN is used?
explanation: VXLAN adds roughly 50 bytes of outer headers to each frame, so a 1500-byte guest frame becomes about 1550 bytes on the wire. Raising the underlay MTU, commonly to 1600, prevents fragmentation or drops for full-size guest traffic.

choices.text: VXLAN encapsulation adds about 50 bytes, so full-size frames need more MTU
VXLAN compresses frames and needs extra headroom for expansion
The virtual switch adds a checksum trailer to every frame
The physical NIC requires an MTU above 1500 to enable VLAN tagging

stem: How does Rapid PVST+ organise its spanning-tree instances?
explanation: Rapid PVST+ runs one 802.1w instance per VLAN, so each VLAN has its own root and its own blocking ports. That allows a different uplink to be active for each VLAN and gives sub-second convergence independently per VLAN.

choices.text: One instance per VLAN, each with its own root bridge
One instance for all VLANs sharing a single root
One instance per physical switch port
One instance per MST region mapped to all VLANs

stem: Which spanning-tree mode is the default on current Cisco IOS switches?
explanation: The default mode is Rapid PVST+ on modern Catalyst platforms. Sending `spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst` is normally redundant, though it is still common in configuration templates and exam answers.

choices.text: Rapid PVST+
PVST+
MST

stem: What VLAN range is allowed on an 802.1Q trunk by default?
explanation: A trunk allows VLANs 1 through 4094 by default, including the reserved and unused IDs in that span. The allowed list can be pruned with `switchport trunk allowed vlan`, but nothing is pruned until that command is issued.

choices.text: 1 through 4094
1 through 1005
1 through 1001
2 through 4094

stem: Which command output confirms that a VLAN is allowed on a trunk and forwarding in the spanning tree?
explanation: The `show interfaces trunk` output lists the allowed VLANs per trunk and, separately, the VLANs that are active and forwarding in spanning tree. Intersecting those two lists is the quickest check that traffic for a VLAN will actually cross the link.

choices.text: show interfaces trunk
show vlan brief
show spanning-tree summary
show interfaces switchport

stem: What is the difference between `switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20` and `switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30`?
explanation: Without the add keyword the command replaces the entire allowed list with the VLANs named. With add it appends to whatever is already permitted, which is why mixing the two forms out of order silently prunes VLANs.

choices.text: The first replaces the allowed list, the second appends to it
The first appends, the second replaces the allowed list
Both append, but the second applies only to new VLANs
The first sets the native VLAN, the second the allowed list

stem: A port mirror session copies traffic from a user port to an analyser. What happens to the original frames?
explanation: SPAN produces a copy while the switch continues to forward the original frame normally to its real destination. Mirroring is passive: it does not redirect, delay beyond normal switching, or alter the original frame in any way.

choices.text: They are still forwarded normally to their real destination
They are dropped after the copy is taken
They are tagged with the mirror VLAN before forwarding
They are held until the analyser acknowledges the copy

stem: A capture configured with two SPAN sources, a host access port and the switch uplink, shows every frame from that host twice. Why?
explanation: Each SPAN source observes the same frame at a different point along its path, once entering the access port and once leaving the uplink. The analyser receives both copies because the switch does not de-duplicate across sources in a session.

choices.text: The same frame is observed at two separate points along its path
The analyser NIC receives both the tagged and untagged copy
SPAN retransmits each frame until it is acknowledged
The uplink mirrors both ingress and egress of every frame

stem: What is the starting point of the shortest path tree that OSPF builds with the SPF algorithm?
explanation: SPF is run over the link-state database with the calculating router itself as the root, and the tree branches outward to every reachable prefix. That is why each router in an area computes a different tree even though all of them hold an identical LSDB.

choices.text: The router running the calculation, as the root of the tree
The area border router for the area
The designated router on the broadcast segment
The router with the lowest router ID in the area

stem: Which OSPF LSA types describe destinations inside the local area, as opposed to those learned from another area?
explanation: Type 1 router LSAs and Type 2 network LSAs stay within an area and describe its internal topology. Type 3 summary LSAs are generated by an ABR to advertise prefixes from one area into another, which is what makes a route inter-area.

choices.text: Type 1 and Type 2 describe intra-area, Type 3 describes inter-area
Type 3 and Type 5 describe intra-area, Type 1 describes inter-area
Type 1 describes intra-area, Type 2 describes external destinations
Type 4 and Type 7 describe intra-area, Type 2 describes inter-area

stem: A router in area 2 must reach an ASBR that sits in area 1. Which OSPF LSA type is flooded into area 2 to advertise the path to that ASBR?
explanation: The Type 4 summary ASBR LSA is generated by the ABR of the area that contains the ASBR and flooded into the other areas, so routers elsewhere know the ASBR is reachable and via which ABR. Type 1 stays inside one area, and the Type 5 external LSAs that describe the redistributed prefixes are unusable without this reachability information.

choices.text: Type 4, the summary ASBR LSA
Type 1, the router LSA
Type 3, the summary network LSA
Type 7, the NSSA external LSA

stem: Two routers on the same segment have different OSPF hello intervals configured. What is the outcome?
explanation: Hello packets are discarded when the interval does not match the locally configured value, so the routers never progress past the down state. The adjacency simply never forms, and no amount of waiting produces a full neighbour relationship.

choices.text: The adjacency never forms because hello packets are rejected
The adjacency forms but stays in two-way state
The adjacency forms and the lower interval is adopted
The adjacency forms only for the backbone area

stem: A router is configured with `network 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 0` while its interface address is 10.1.1.5/24. What does the network command actually do?
explanation: The network command is a selector, not an advertisement: it enables OSPF on every interface whose address falls inside the range. The prefix placed into OSPF is the interface actual subnet, so 10.1.1.0/24 is advertised because the interface is /24, not because of the mask in the command.

choices.text: It enables OSPF on interfaces whose addresses fall inside the range
It advertises exactly the prefix written in the command
It creates a static route for that range in area 0
It restricts OSPF to neighbours inside that range

stem: In which OSPF neighbour state have master and slave been elected and database description packets been exchanged, but link-state requests not yet sent?
explanation: Exchange is the state where the routers swap DBD packets to compare their databases while master and slave roles are already settled. Once the comparison finishes they move to Loading and send link-state requests for the missing entries, then to Full.

choices.text: Exchange
ExStart
Loading
Two-way

stem: Two eBGP speakers are separated by two routers. What must be configured for the session to come up?
explanation: eBGP sets a TTL of 1 on its packets, so a peer that is not directly connected never receives them. `neighbor x.x.x.x ebgp-multihop 2` raises the TTL enough for the session to survive the intermediate hops.

choices.text: The ebgp-multihop option, because eBGP sends with a TTL of 1
A static route to the peer, because eBGP ignores routing tables
The next-hop-self option, because eBGP rewrites next hops
A route reflector, because eBGP cannot peer across routers

stem: How is the BGP router ID chosen when it is not configured manually?
explanation: BGP prefers the highest IP address on a loopback interface and falls back to the highest IP address on any active physical interface. The value is fixed when the session is established, so changing addresses later does not move it until BGP is reset.

choices.text: Highest loopback address, otherwise the highest physical interface address
Lowest loopback address, otherwise the lowest physical interface address
Highest physical interface address, otherwise the lowest loopback
The address of the interface used to reach the first peer

stem: An EIGRP router sends a query and receives no reply before the active timer expires. What happens?
explanation: The route is declared stuck in active and the router resets the neighbour that failed to answer, which tears down the adjacency. The route then goes unreachable until the neighbour comes back and the topology is relearned.

choices.text: The route is declared stuck in active and the non-responding neighbour is reset
The route is marked passive and kept in the routing table
The router floods a new query with a longer timeout
The route is replaced by the feasible successor without a reset

stem: What does the EIGRP topology table store for each destination?
explanation: The topology table keeps every successor and feasible successor along with the reported distance each neighbour advertised and the locally computed feasible distance. That stored detail is what allows an immediate switch to a feasible successor when the best path fails.

choices.text: Feasible successors along with reported and feasible distances
Only the single best route installed in the routing table
The raw hello and query packets received from neighbours
The link-state database for the autonomous system

stem: Which syslog severity level corresponds to the number 5?
explanation: Numbering runs from 0 (emergencies) to 7 (debugging), so 5 is notice. Notice covers normal but significant conditions, one step less urgent than warning at 4 and one step more urgent than informational at 6.

choices.text: Notice
Warning
Informational
Error

stem: Which SNMP operation does an SNMP walk repeatedly use to retrieve a subtree of the MIB?
explanation: A walk issues GETNEXT requests, each time asking for the object that follows the last one returned, until the agent reports that the subtree is exhausted. GETBULK is the bulk variant, but the classic walk is built from successive GETNEXT calls.

choices.text: GETNEXT
GET
SET
TRAP

stem: Which command generates a 2048-bit RSA key pair for SSH on a Cisco router?
explanation: The modulus keyword sets the key length, so `crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048` creates a 2048-bit pair. The keys must exist before SSH version 2 can be enabled, and the domain name must already be configured.

choices.text: crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
crypto key generate rsa 2048
ssh key generate rsa 2048
ip ssh key modulus 2048

stem: A guest WLAN is enabled with client isolation. What does that prevent?
explanation: Client isolation blocks direct traffic between wireless clients associated to the same SSID or VLAN. Guests can still reach the default gateway and the internet, but cannot attack or scan each other, which is the main reason it is enabled on guest networks.

choices.text: Guest clients from reaching each other directly
Guest clients from reaching the default gateway
Guest clients from obtaining a DHCP address
Guest clients from associating to the SSID

stem: An RA Guard policy is applied with the monitor keyword. What is the effect on router advertisement messages received on the port?
explanation: Monitor mode logs and counts the messages that would have been dropped but still forwards them. It is used to baseline a network before enforcing the policy, so legitimate router ports are identified without breaking IPv6 connectivity.

choices.text: They are logged and permitted rather than dropped
They are dropped and logged
They are dropped without being logged
They are rewritten with the switch own prefix

stem: What does the TTL value in a DNS record control?
explanation: The TTL tells a caching resolver how many seconds it may keep the answer before querying again. A short TTL makes record changes propagate quickly at the cost of more queries; a long TTL reduces query load but delays updates.

choices.text: How long a resolver may cache the answer before re-querying
How long the authoritative server keeps the zone in memory
How often the client renews its DHCP lease
How long a TCP connection to the server stays open

stem: Which configuration hardens the auxiliary port on a router that is not used for out-of-band access?
explanation: Entering `line aux 0` and disabling exec with `no exec` prevents anyone from getting a prompt over that line, and `transport input none` blocks protocol access entirely. The console port should still be protected with a password under `line con 0`.

choices.text: line aux 0, then no exec and transport input none
line con 0, then no exec and transport input none
line vty 0 4, then no exec
interface aux 0, then shutdown

stem: Which set of data sources does an AIOps platform typically correlate to detect and explain incidents?
explanation: AIOps combines telemetry and metrics, syslog and event streams, flow records, configuration state, and ticketing or change history. Correlating them lets the platform link a symptom to the change or configuration drift that caused it, instead of alerting on each stream in isolation.

choices.text: Telemetry, logs, flow records, configuration, and change tickets
Only SNMP traps from the network devices
Only the configuration archive from the devices
Only user tickets raised with the service desk

stem: An automation agent is given the raw output of `show running-config` and asked to propose changes. How should that output be treated?
explanation: Device output is untrusted data, so text inside a banner or description could contain instructions aimed at the model. The agent must treat the content as data to analyse, never as commands, and any proposed change must be validated before it is applied to a device.

choices.text: As untrusted data that must be validated, not as instructions to follow
As trusted configuration that can be applied as returned
As a prompt that the model should execute verbatim
As a schema that defines which commands are permitted
